title: Joshua
subtitle: Into the land
lead: The book of Joshua is named for its hero, Joshua son of Nun, Moses' assistant and successor. His Hebrew name, Yehoshua, means "the LORD saves"; shortened to Yeshua and written Iesous in Greek, it is the same name as Jesus. The book picks up where Deuteronomy ends: "After the death of Moses the servant of the LORD" (1:1). In the Hebrew Bible it is the first of the Former Prophets (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings), the history that runs from the entry into the land to the exile.

The book has two halves. Chapters 1–12 tell how Israel crossed the Jordan and took the land: Rahab and the spies, the river standing in a heap, circumcision and Passover at Gilgal, the fall of Jericho, Achan's sin and the defeat and capture of Ai, the altar on Mount Ebal, the Gibeonites' trick, the day the sun stood still, and the northern war against Hazor, ending with a list of thirty-one defeated kings. Chapters 13–24 tell how the land was divided among the tribes, with towns of refuge and towns for the Levites, and end with the eastern tribes' altar, Joshua's farewell, and the covenant at Shechem.

Joshua is a book of promises kept: "Not one of all the good words the LORD had spoken to the house of Israel fell short" (21:45). It is also one of the hardest books in the Bible for modern readers, because it tells of whole towns "put under the ban" and destroyed at God's command. Jews and Christians have read it as history, as a call to faithfulness, as a picture of spiritual warfare and rest, and as a text to wrestle with. This study presents those readings side by side, along with what archaeology has and has not found.
facts: Not named. Jewish tradition (Bavli Bava Batra 15a): Joshua, with the account of his death added by Eleazar and Phinehas. Most critical scholars: the Deuteronomistic writers of the 7th and 6th centuries BC, using older sources.
Set in the late Bronze Age, either about 1406 BC (early date) or the 13th century BC (late date). Critical: written down mainly between about 620 and 550 BC.
The Jordan Valley, Jericho, Ai, Gibeon, Shechem and the hill country, the south (Negev and Shephelah), and the north around Hazor
History told as story, with battle reports, lists of kings and borders, speeches, and a covenant ceremony

audience.to: Israelites living in the land long after the conquest. They knew its towns, its ruins and its stone heaps "to this day." Who they were depends on the view of authorship. On the traditional view, they were Israel in the generations after Joshua. On the critical view, they were first the people of Judah under King Josiah about 620 BC, who hoped to win back the north. Then they were the exiles in Babylon after 586 BC, who had lost the land. Some think priestly editors were still shaping the book for Jews in Persian times.
audience.why: To show that the LORD kept his promise of the land, and that Israel holds it only by keeping the written law of Moses. The book opens with the command to keep the scroll of the law day and night (1:8). It closes with the people choosing to serve the LORD at Shechem (24:15–24). Its stories of Rahab and the Gibeonites show outsiders joining Israel, while Achan shows an insider lost through greed. Knowing the audience changes the reading. For people already in the land, it is a call to loyalty. For a king hoping to restore all Israel, it is a model of one people under one law. For exiles, it is a reminder of what was lost. It is also a promise that God's words do not fail (21:45; 23:14–16).
views: The Talmud says Joshua wrote the book, with its last verses added by Eleazar and Phinehas (Bavli Bava Batra 15a). The first readers would be the generation that settled the land, who could still see the memorials and meet Rahab's family (6:25). Conservative scholars such as Woudstra and Hess think the book rests on early records, updated by later editors.

Cross and others see a first edition of the history from Deuteronomy to Kings under Josiah. Joshua reads the law to all Israel and leads one people to take the whole land. In this he mirrors Josiah. Josiah read the scroll to the people, made a covenant, and pushed into the old northern territory (2 Kings 23:1–3, 15–20).

Noth argued that the whole history was written in the exile to explain why Israel lost the land. Chapter 23 warns that Israel will vanish from the good land if it serves other gods. On this view the warning speaks straight to exiles who had seen it happen.

Many scholars find priestly material in chapters 13–22, such as the tent at Shiloh, Eleazar the priest and the altar by the Jordan. The Greek and the Hebrew editions also differ. On this view the book was still growing in Persian and Hellenistic times, for Jews in Yehud and abroad who asked who belonged to Israel and where it could worship.

Many archaeologists find little evidence for a swift conquest in the late Bronze Age. They read the book as a theological history built on local traditions. Others, such as Kitchen and Hoffmeier, compare its battle reports with ancient conquest accounts, which are often stylized and overstated.

lenses.name: History as told
lenses.desc: The traditional reading, Jewish and Christian: Israel crossed the Jordan under Joshua and took Canaan in the late Bronze Age, whether in the 15th century BC (the early date) or the 13th (the late date). Many who hold this view note that the book itself says much of the land was left unconquered (13:1).

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Most academic scholars read Joshua as part of the Deuteronomistic History, written centuries later. They point to sites like Jericho and Ai that show little or no occupation at the right time, and they favor models of slow settlement or of Israel emerging from within Canaan.

lenses.name: Ethics of conquest
lenses.desc: Jewish, Christian and secular readers wrestle with the ban (cherem) and the killing of whole towns: some read it as hyperbole in ancient war rhetoric (Wolterstorff, Copan), some as a unique divine judgment, and some as a text to argue with.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: Joshua is the first of the Former Prophets. The Talmud credits him with writing it (Bava Batra 14b–15a), and the rabbis read the land promise, the sun standing still and Rahab, who they say married Joshua, as lessons for later generations.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Joshua shares the name Jesus (Yeshua; the Greek is Iesous). The New Testament praises Rahab's faith and works (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25) and reads the rest Joshua did not finally give as pointing to a greater rest (Hebrews 4:8).

authorship: Traditional view: Joshua and his successors

The Talmud says that "Joshua wrote his book and eight verses of the Torah," the last eight verses of Deuteronomy, and that Eleazar and Phinehas added the account of his death (Bavli Bava Batra 15a). The book says that Joshua wrote words "in the book of God's law" (24:26), and the note that Rahab "has lived among Israel to this day" (6:25) suggests a writer within her lifetime. Conservative scholars such as Marten Woudstra, Richard Hess and Kenneth Kitchen hold that the book rests on early records, with some updating by later editors, as the many notes "to this day" show.

Martin Noth (1943) argued that Joshua is part of one history, written in the exile in the style and with the values of Deuteronomy, running from Deuteronomy to Kings. Frank Moore Cross and others see a first edition under King Josiah (about 620 BC), when Judah hoped to retake the north, and a second in the exile. On this view Joshua's speeches (chapters 1, 23) and its stress on the written law are the editors' work, while the stories behind chapters 2–11 come from older local traditions, many tied to the shrine at Gilgal and to the tribe of Benjamin.

Older critics, following Julius Wellhausen, read Joshua as the end of the Pentateuch's sources, a "Hexateuch" of six books in which the promise of land made in Genesis is fulfilled. This view is less common now, but many scholars still see priestly material in chapters 13–22.

The Septuagint of Joshua differs from the Hebrew in hundreds of places and is about four to five percent shorter. Emanuel Tov, A. Graeme Auld and others argue that it was translated from an older Hebrew edition, so that the book was still growing in the last centuries BC. A Dead Sea Scroll, 4QJosh-a, places the altar scene of 8:30–35 right after the crossing. Others think the Greek translator shortened and rearranged his text.

Plain English Translation

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level, built line by line from the Hebrew words rather than adapted from another English version. YHWH is "the LORD," and Adonai YHWH is "Lord GOD" (7:7). Key terms are kept steady across the whole Bible: cherem is "under the ban" (devoted to destruction); yarash is "take possession of" a land or "drive out" a people; nachalah is "inheritance"; hesed is "loyal love"; ger is "foreigner" or "foreigner who lives among you"; torah is "law"; hakkohanim halwiyyim are "the Levite priests"; eved is "servant" or "slave" by context. Where the Septuagint or a Dead Sea Scroll differs in a way that matters, the variant can be shown in place.

Other translations

The Berean Standard Bible (2023), the King James Version (1611/1769), the American Standard Version (1901), Young's Literal Translation (1898) and the World English Bible can be shown for comparison. The KJV sometimes follows the written Hebrew where modern versions follow the marginal reading (for example 5:1, "until we were passed over").

The book falls into two halves joined by summaries. Taking the land (chapters 1–12): the charge to Joshua (1); spies and Rahab (2); the crossing and the stones (3–4); circumcision, Passover and the commander of the army (5); Jericho (6); Achan and Ai (7–8), with the altar on Ebal (8:30–35); Gibeon (9); the southern campaign and the long day (10); the northern campaign and the summary (11); the list of kings (12). Dividing the land (chapters 13–21): land still to take and the eastern tribes (13); Caleb (14); Judah (15); Joseph's tribes (16–17); Shiloh and the seven remaining tribes (18–19); towns of refuge (20) and Levites (21), ending "every promise was kept" (21:43–45). Keeping the land (chapters 22–24): the eastern altar (22), Joshua's farewell (23), and the covenant at Shechem (24). Many scholars see the book framed by speeches at its start and end (1 and 23–24), in Deuteronomy's style.

Readers divide sharply on how the conquest stories relate to what happened. The conquest model, held by traditional readers and, in the mid-20th century, by William F. Albright and his school, takes the book as a record of a swift military campaign, pointing to destruction layers at Hazor and other sites. The peaceful infiltration model of Albrecht Alt and Martin Noth saw Israel's tribes settling gradually in the empty hills. The revolt model of George Mendenhall and Norman Gottwald saw Israel arising from Canaanite peasants who threw off their city-state kings. Most archaeologists today, such as Israel Finkelstein and William Dever, see Israel emerging mainly from within Canaan, in hundreds of small hill villages that appeared after about 1200 BC. Problems for a literal reading include Jericho and Ai, which show little or no occupation at the likely times, and Gibeon. Defenders of the book's history answer that many sites are uncertain, that the book says only three towns were burned (11:13), that its war language is stylized, and that the early date fits some of the evidence. Joshua itself contains both a picture of total conquest (11:23) and a picture of incomplete settlement (13:1; 15:63; 17:12), which Judges 1 continues.

No book of the Bible raises the problem of divine violence more sharply. Readers have answered in several ways, all represented on this site. Some hold that the conquest was a unique act of judgment on societies whose guilt was "full" (Genesis 15:16), commanded once and never to be repeated; Israel itself is warned that the land will vomit it out for the same sins (Leviticus 18:24–28), and the Wisdom of Solomon says God judged the Canaanites little by little to give them room to repent (Wisdom 12:3–11). Some, such as Kenneth Kitchen, K. Lawson Younger, Nicholas Wolterstorff, Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan, argue that the language of total destruction is ancient war rhetoric, and that the book itself shows Canaanites remaining. A related argument notes that the main commands are to "drive out" and "take possession" (Exodus 23:28–30; Deuteronomy 7:20), not to annihilate, and that the ban falls mainly on fortified royal towns (Copan and Flannagan; John and Harvey Walton). Many critical scholars hold that the campaigns are largely literary and were written to teach exclusive loyalty to the LORD. Others, such as Eric Seibert and Gregory Boyd, read the texts in light of Jesus and judge their picture of God as partial. Native American, Palestinian and other readers have shown how these stories were used to justify taking land, and ask that the book be read with that history in view. Inside the book, Rahab and the Gibeonites show that the line between Israel and Canaan could be crossed.

Joshua opens the Prophets, and passages from it are read in synagogue as haftarot: chapter 1 on Simchat Torah, when the reading of the Torah ends and begins again, and chapter 2 with the portion of the spies (Numbers 13–15). The rabbis made Joshua the link in the chain of tradition from Moses (Mishnah Avot 1:1), honored Rahab as a righteous convert and Joshua's wife, and held that Joshua offered the Canaanites peace before war, sending them a choice to leave, make peace or fight (Jerusalem Talmud Shevi'it 6:1). Here Jewish tradition is divided: the Sifre and Rashi limit the offer of peace in Deuteronomy 20:10 to distant towns, while Nachmanides and Maimonides held that it was offered even to the seven nations, on condition that they keep the Noahide laws and accept tribute and service (Laws of Kings 6:1–5). In modern times the book has been read both as a charter for the land of Israel and, by others, as a warning against reading ancient wars as present commands.

For Christians, Joshua's name points to Jesus, who leads God's people into their inheritance; the Greek of Hebrews 4:8 calls him Iesous. The New Testament praises Rahab's faith (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25), names her in Jesus' family (Matthew 1:5), and reads the rest Joshua gave as a foretaste of a greater rest (Hebrews 4:1–11). From Origen's Homilies on Joshua on, many Christians read the wars as a picture of the soul's struggle against sin, with the Canaanites as vices; the Jordan became a picture of baptism and of death. Calvin and other Reformers read the book more historically and defended God's justice in the conquest. In modern times the book has been used both to inspire perseverance and, sadly, to justify colonial conquest, and many Christian scholars now read it with that history in mind.

Joshua has one of the most interesting textual histories in the Old Testament. The Septuagint is shorter by about four to five percent, lacks several verses (8:11b–13; 8:26; 10:15; 10:43), places the altar on Ebal after 9:2, tells the circumcision of 5:4–6 differently, and adds verses at 6:26 and after 24:30 (Joshua's flint knives buried with him) and 24:33. Two Dead Sea Scrolls, 4QJosh-a and 4QJosh-b, preserve fragments; 4QJosh-a places the first altar at Gilgal, right after the crossing. Scholars debate whether the Greek reflects an older Hebrew edition (Tov, Auld) or a translator's freedom (van der Meer). The variants are shown in place on the text pages.

spec.title: Joshua as a book about two kinds of crossing
spec.body: My own reading of the whole book: Joshua is built around crossings of boundaries. Israel crosses the Jordan into the land, and outsiders cross into Israel: Rahab (chapter 2), the foreigners at Ebal (8:33), the Gibeonites (chapter 9), Caleb the Kenizzite, an outsider by birth who receives Hebron (14:6–15). Meanwhile insiders cross out: Achan of Judah becomes "something under the ban" (chapter 7), and the eastern tribes' altar raises the fear that the Jordan will divide Israel (chapter 22). The book ends with a call to choose whom to serve (24:15). I suggest that this two-way traffic is the book's own answer to its violence: the real boundary of Israel is loyalty to the LORD, not blood or geography. Several scholars, especially L. Daniel Hawk and Richard Nelson, have written about insiders and outsiders in Joshua; the idea that the book is designed around paired crossings is my own.

reading: A clear critical commentary, strong on the book's literary art and its textual history.
Richard S. Hess, Joshua (Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries, 1996)
A short evangelical commentary with good use of archaeology and ancient Near Eastern texts.
A detailed critical commentary that pays close attention to the Greek text.
A literary reading that brings out the book's tensions, ironies and outsiders.
K. Lawson Younger Jr., Ancient Conquest Accounts (1990)
Compares Joshua 9–12 with Assyrian, Hittite and Egyptian war reports.
Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan, Did God Really Command Genocide? (2014)
A Christian philosophical defense of reading the conquest as hyperbole and judgment.
Eric A. Seibert, The Violence of Scripture (2012)
Argues for reading the Old Testament's violent texts critically in light of Jesus.
Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman, The Bible Unearthed (2001)
A popular presentation of the archaeological case that Israel emerged from within Canaan.

traditions.q: Do Joshua's wars give Christians any warrant to fight in war?
views: The conquest was a unique command tied to God's judgment and is not a model for today. A nation may still defend itself by force, but only under the strict conditions of a just war: a grave and certain wrong, a last resort, a real hope of success, and no greater evil caused (Catechism 2307–2317; Thomas Aquinas, Summa II-II q40).

The Orthodox Church honors soldiers who defend the innocent but has never called war good in itself. Basil the Great advised that soldiers who had killed in war keep away from Communion for three years, because even necessary killing wounds the soul (Letter 188, canon 13).

Christians may serve as soldiers and fight in just wars, because the sword belongs to the God-given office of government, not to private revenge (Augsburg Confession 16). Luther wrote that a soldier who protects his neighbors can do a work of love (Whether Soldiers, Too, Can Be Saved).

Christian rulers may wage war on just and necessary occasions (Westminster Confession 23.2). Calvin read Joshua's wars as God's own judgment, carried out at his command, and so not a pattern any ruler may copy on his own authority.

Followers of Jesus must not use the sword at all; the Schleitheim Confession (article 6) calls it outside the perfection of Christ. Mennonites read Joshua in the light of Jesus' command to love enemies (Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective, article 22).
The Quaker peace testimony of 1660 rejects all outward wars and fighting, for any purpose. Quakers read the Old Testament wars as belonging to a time before Christ, whose Spirit leads away from war.
